cards.title: Legislative Intelligence Platform
questions: tell me about the legislation project

cards.title: Bill passage prediction
questions: how accurate is the bill prediction model
can you predict which bills pass
how did you validate the model
what went wrong with the training data
cards.answer: I built a bill passage prediction model using 117,722 bills, fixing train/serve skew with a shared input module and verifying 36,028 inputs were byte-identical. Adding each bill's title and synopsis improved the introduction-time ROC-AUC from 0.561 to 0.845, confirmed by ablation and leakage checks. On a held-out 103rd General Assembly, at a 0.70 threshold, the model achieved 75.1% precision and 76.2% recall, with a median of 21 days' warning before the floor vote.

cards.title: UIC enrollment forecasting

I initiated the project, brought together interns and staff, tested approaches, and presented findings to UIC leadership.

cards.title: Email archiving and PII anonymization
cards.answer: I processed 79,676 historical emails from a 20-year institutional archive using Microsoft Presidio to detect and anonymize PII with five strategies. I used LLaMA for de-identified summaries and LDA plus LLM labels to extract topics. The project, built with RIMS and the University Library, enables opening historical correspondence to researchers while keeping sensitive data protected.

cards.title: Archival image intelligence

cards.title: vLLM vs Ollama throughput evaluation
questions: how did you speed up inference
cards.answer: I ran a controlled benchmark comparing vLLM and Ollama on a single NVIDIA L4 GPU using the same model architecture. The bottleneck was Ollama’s request serialization, not the hardware or model. Switching to vLLM’s continuous batching gave a 6.22x speedup at concurrency 8, dropping a 12,125-image task from 22 hours to 3.7 hours. GPU utilization rose from 28% to 97%.

cards.title: vLLM multi-model sweep (legislation pipeline)

Llama 3.1 8B AWQ at chunk size 1200 led by over 20 parse-OK points and held quality under load. Human review showed parse-OK alone could be misleading, a nuance I explored in a Medium post.

cards.title: Procurement intelligence

It uses exact part-number matching, FAISS semantic retrieval over 5.19 million embeddings, and LLM equivalence reasoning to identify savings. After correcting for 49.1% pack-size inflation, it found $161,564 in defensible unit-normalized savings. The system includes a price comparison tool and a spending dashboard for leadership.

cards.title: The root cause of agent failure
questions: what do you think most ai projects get wrong?
why don't agents work in production
cards.answer: Most failures come from one assumption: the model is smart enough to handle everything. It's not. Not yet. The systems that work handle preprocessing upfront, clean and structure data, provide schema-level context, design retrieval carefully, and use prompts that preserve context and coherence. Fix the system around the model and the model performs dramatically better.

cards.title: Agent, workflow or RPA?
questions: how do you choose between a simple model and a complex one?
when should you use an ai agent
when not to use an agent
do i need an agent or a script
where do you draw the line between agents and pipelines
is an llm agent overkill for this
cards.answer: Agent territory: ambiguous decisions, logical reasoning, evolving inputs. The example I use is scraping trending topics in news. You can't hard-code what's trending, it changes constantly, and the model has to look at generalities and pick top themes. That's genuine agent work. Workflow automation: static process, consistent algorithm, consistent input and output. Same shape data coming in, same shape data going out. Don't use an agent for that. RPA: the simplest stuff, standard ETL, standard in and standard out. Old-school data science methods handle this perfectly. You don't need an AI agent. Rule of thumb: if the task requires the system to interpret something that isn't clearly defined, it's an agent. If it doesn't, it isn't, and forcing AI into it just adds complexity and cost.

cards.title: Are AI agents a real paradigm shift?
questions: what do you think ai will do to the world over the next 10 to 20 years?
are ai agents a paradigm shift
are agents just automation with better ux
what is different about ai agents
will agents change how we work
cards.answer: Yes. I don't think agents are just an evolution of automation and APIs with better UX. They're a real shift in how work gets done. The part that's fundamentally different is ambiguity. Traditional pipelines follow deterministic logic, rule-based, conditional, predictable in. Agents operate where the decision isn't something you can hard-code. Where the model has to make a judgment call on fuzzy inputs. That's both the power and the risk. You're handing off the ambiguity to the AI, and whatever it decides is what happens next. If you think your role is safe, it probably isn't. Within the next 6 to 12 months, tasks, not whole jobs, but tasks, are going to start getting stripped out of roles at an accelerating pace. Whether that's a problem depends on your job. If it's mostly repetitive, yeah, be concerned. If it involves real decision-making, stakeholder work, strategy, and business impact, you're likely fine, but your job will evolve.

cards.title: The non-negotiable in an agent system
questions: how do you design a system that fails safely and tells you when it fails?
what is non-negotiable when designing an agent system
how do you stop ai drift
how do you anchor llm outputs to truth
how do you detect model drift
old school and new school validation
what does every agent system need
cards.answer: There has to be a way to anchor outputs back to truth. AI systems drift. The more they build on prior outputs, the worse it gets. So you need a base truth layer, validated data, known-good outputs, plus a way to detect drift and cross-check results. Some tolerance for variation is fine. Unlimited deviation isn't. My concrete example: in my legislation work, I have the Llama model generating category labels (new-school) and I also have an old-school clustering model generating categories from keywords (old-school). Both produce taxonomies. If one says Higher Education and the other says K-12 for the same bill, that's a flag. I can isolate the mismatches, inspect them, and figure out whether the model drifted or the data is weird. Hybrid validation like that is essential.

cards.title: If AI is doing it, make it auditable
questions: how do you decide whether an ai system is good enough to ship? how do you know it works?
how do you trust ai output
can ai clean my data and make a report
cards.answer: A lot of what people want to use AI for, they shouldn't. Example: 'here's a bunch of data, clean it and generate a report.' That's not reliable. If AI is going to do it, it should generate the code that did it and show everything that's auditable about how it reached its conclusion. Then you double-check the data, double-check the calculations. AI-generated deterministic code you can read and trust beats an agent black-boxing it every single time.

cards.title: Augmentation and replacement at the same time
questions: what harms of ai worry you most, and what should we do about them?
does ai augment or replace people
should humans stay in the loop
who should make decisions about people
should ai decide who gets hired
cards.answer: Everyone says 'AI augments humans' but most of the time that's vague or not really true. Both are happening simultaneously. The difference is what kind of work and how much oversight exists. Real augmentation: AI helps you move faster, you still own the outcome. You review, validate, correct, make the final call. AI accelerates, humans stay responsible for correctness. Where humans must stay in control right now: hiring, firing, legal outcomes, financial decisions, anything that directly affects someone's life. Those need multiple layers of review: the person who built the system approves how it works, stakeholders own the decisions, and someone audits continuously. Without that, it's not augmentation, it's uncontrolled automation in a trench coat.

cards.title: Bundled prompts beat isolated prompts
questions: how do you evaluate an llm or a rag system? what metrics do you trust?
should i ask one question per prompt
how do you design prompts for extraction
cards.answer: When I was extracting 10+ structured features from legislation text, I originally thought asking each question separately would make parsing cleaner and more predictable. Turns out that's wrong. Bundling the questions in the same prompt gave better results because the model uses its earlier answers as context for later ones. If it already established 'this impacts higher education' and 'this affects students,' then when I later ask 'does this impact the university,' it answers yes coherently, and when I ask 'rate the impact as slight/moderate/very impactful,' it uses everything it just figured out. Context builds within the prompt. Isolating tasks too much loses coherence and reasoning continuity. Prompt engineering isn't just asking questions, it's designing the context the model reasons inside.

cards.title: What context actually means in production
questions: how do you evaluate an llm or a rag system? what metrics do you trust?
what does context mean in ai
why do production ai systems fail
what is context in an llm system
is context more important than the model
tags: context matters more than the model
cards.answer: When people say 'context,' they usually mean something vague. In production it's very concrete. It breaks into four things: data quality, retrieval, schema (does the system understand what the data means), and memory (how information carries across tasks). If any one of those is weak, the system fails. This is my territory and I don't stay surface-level on it. Context is where most agent failures actually happen, not the model.

cards.title: Is data science dying?
questions: what's a technical opinion you hold that many of your peers disagree with?
is traditional data science irrelevant now
cards.answer: There's a narrative that traditional data science is becoming irrelevant. I disagree. It's becoming a validation layer for AI systems. Clustering, statistical methods, structured models, they're how you ground outputs, detect inconsistency, and stay reliable. The more powerful the generative system, the more you need the boring methods behind it to catch when things drift.

cards.title: What energizes me
questions: what kind of problems do you love working on? what makes a problem interesting to you?
what kind of problems do you love
cards.answer: People analytics. Behavioral analytics. Sentiment. Network graphs of motivation and intent. Understanding what's happening below the surface of what people say and do, and using that to predict what comes next. Anything that helps me understand humans better.

cards.title: The entry-level job market
questions: what advice would you give someone afraid of losing their job to ai?
is the junior job market broken
is it hard to get a junior job
cards.answer: Short term, the weakest spot in the job market is entry-level. Companies don't need as many junior hires for basic tasks. AI tools let existing employees absorb that work. So instead of hiring a new grad, companies redistribute internally. But here's the contradiction: entry-level capability is actually higher than it's been in years. A fresh grad today can build faster, learn faster, and produce higher-quality work earlier than anyone four years ago. So my take is: if you need someone for straightforward work, just hire them. Don't overcomplicate hiring with unnecessary technical challenges. Every senior is using AI to write code. Every company has token quotas for productivity. Why are we putting juniors through loops we don't put ourselves through?

cards.title: What excites me about AI
questions: are you an ai optimist or pessimist, and why?
best thing about ai right now
why are you excited about ai
cards.answer: The barrier to building has collapsed. If you can dream it, you can build it. More people than ever can turn ideas into real things. Yes, there's a ton of AI slop, but there will also be people using these tools for genuinely world-changing work. That's worth being excited about. It's also worth being cautious about. Both can be true.

cards.title: AI and financial data
questions: what harms of ai worry you most, and what should we do about them?
is ai good with financial data
could ai pass an accounting exam
cards.answer: I had a professor who teaches accounting tell me this: if you gave AI the midterms or finals for an accounting class, it'd get about 70% right, as it stands. That's not good enough for anything real. Financial data, multi-step conditional logic, complex calculations, AI still struggles. Use it to get closer to where you need to go, not to own the final answer. It'll get better, we'll get there, but 'there' isn't today.

cards.title: Where should a company start with AI?
questions: what do you think most ai projects get wrong?
where should a company start with ai
how to pick an ai use case
cards.answer: There's no universal 'best first use case.' It's entirely individual to the business. The real questions are: where are the bottlenecks? What takes too long today that you can't process fast enough? What would generate real value if you could do it quickly, often, and at scale? Every company is different. The answer is always wherever there's a painful bottleneck with real value on the other side. Anyone giving you a generic answer isn't thinking about your business. They're selling you something.

cards.title: The rise of the jack-of-all-trades
questions: what advice would you give someone afraid of losing their job to ai?
will one person do the work of five
what kind of worker wins with ai
cards.answer: We're moving toward a different kind of worker, someone who can do a little bit of everything, efficiently. Learning new skills is faster than ever. AI lowers the barrier to execution. One person can cover multiple functions. Fewer people are needed, and each person is expected to do more. In some cases one person will effectively do the work of what used to take five. That's where the advantage is, being the person who can absorb multiple roles.

cards.title: What good work means to me
questions: what does good work mean to you?
what does good work mean to you
how do you define quality work
what does good look like to you
cards.answer: Good work isn't just that it functions. It's documented so others can pick it up. It fits into a larger ecosystem. It drives actionable insight. And intrinsically, it's good, a fair win for everyone involved, not just profit-extracting. Works technically + works in context + does actual good = good work.

cards.title: The hard truth about AI implementation
questions: what do you think most ai projects get wrong?
what don't people want to hear about ai
cards.answer: People don't want to deal with their data. They want instant gratification. They want magical outputs with zero effort. But if your data is bad, AI won't fix it for you. It'll just produce plausible-looking garbage on top of it, faster.

cards.title: Which jobs are most at risk
questions: what advice would you give someone afraid of losing their job to ai?
which jobs are most at risk from ai
is my job safe from ai
which careers are safe from ai
what work will be automated first
cards.answer: Anything repetitive and rules-based. Basic SQL querying, simple ETL and RPA-style workflows, entry-level coding and analysis. If the work is predictable, structured, and repeatable, it's at high risk of automation. The exceptions are roles that involve ambiguity, relationships, decision-making, and business judgment.

cards.title: How to kill 80% of AI projects
questions: what do you think most ai projects get wrong?
how do you decide which ai projects to kill
which ai projects should we cancel
two questions before any ai project
what to ask before starting an ai project
cards.answer: Two criteria. Real business impact, and data that's actually ready. If either is no, the project shouldn't exist. That's it. Prioritization of those two things is the whole game.

cards.title: How I approach messy data
questions: how do you approach a problem nobody has solved before? walk through your process.
how do you approach a messy dataset
where do you start with messy data
how do you tackle dirty data
first steps with a messy data set
cards.answer: I don't start by cleaning line by line. I start by understanding structure. Cluster first, look for what naturally groups, then see where things break. The outliers are usually more interesting than the main groups because they tell you where the data is failing. If I find myself adding more and more one-off rules, that's the signal the problem isn't fixable in a meaningful way. At that point you're duct-taping, not standardizing.

cards.title: What motivates me
questions: why do you do this work
what gets you up in the morning
why do you love this work
cards.answer: Driving impact and being ahead of the curve. I get excited about using new tech to do what wasn't possible before. I like to wow people.

cards.title: Favorite movies
questions: what do you do for fun: hobbies, art, outdoors?
cards.answer: Lord of the Rings, The Fifth Element, Young Frankenstein, The Princess Bride. Also Step Brothers and Scrooged for comedies/Christmas.

cards.title: When I'd refuse a closed model, and when I'd refuse open source
questions: local open-weights models versus cloud apis: when do you choose which?
when would you refuse to use a closed model
when not to use open source
cards.answer: If I needed something tracking behavior over time, or being updated with live trends, or where deeper control over behavior matters, closed systems limit flexibility in ways that can quietly hurt you. Cloud-based closed models are also problematic for use cases where I need guarantees about what's happening with the data. Anything involving private or sensitive data that shouldn't be leaving a controlled environment. If it's PII, legislation with exposure risk, or anything high-stakes and private, I'd containerize the model on an on-prem server and wouldn't involve third-party services. The trade-off is less raw model power, but for a lot of tasks that's fine.

cards.title: The outlier bills that broke my pipeline
questions: what's the hardest bug or production issue you've debugged?
a war story from your pipelines
giant bills that broke the pipeline
cards.answer: In my legislation work, some bills were massive outliers, over 100,000 tokens, roughly 100x the size of a normal bill. Only about 5% of the data, but they added enormous noise. They were amendment-heavy bills, the same content updated over and over with every small change. Most of it added no context. What actually mattered was the latest changes, maybe the last thousand tokens. If you feed those directly into an AI system without preprocessing, it chunks them inefficiently, wastes compute, takes hours to process the worst-quality subset, and pollutes everything downstream. The fix wasn't an AI fix. It was a preprocessing fix. Detect the outliers, summarize them as 'amendment type, last changes attached,' and move on. Good data preprocessing should never be wasted AI logic.

cards.title: The most overhyped AI claim: text to SQL
questions: what's a technical opinion you hold that many of your peers disagree with?
what is the most overhyped thing in ai
can you trust sql written by ai
cards.answer: The most overhyped thing in AI right now is that you can just throw all your data into something, use text-to-SQL, and get a report you can actually trust and act on. It's not there. People are jumping over fundamentals. Data is messy, inconsistent, poorly structured, and everyone's trying to skip the preprocessing and cleaning. Cool demos, consistent production failure. We need 2 to 3 years for companies that start now, maybe 5 for the stragglers. Want AI to do the magical stuff? Start with your data today.

cards.title: Long term, value shifts back to the human stuff
questions: what will humans be valued for once ai can do most knowledge work?
what happens when ai does all the work
will live music and art matter more
will we value human made things
what will be left for humans to do
what do humans do if ai does everything
cards.answer: If AI handles most of the work, what do humans do? It could be doom and gloom, or it could be a return to valuing what's actually human. I'm betting on the second one. Human-created art. Live music in a hot crowded venue with a sweaty microphone. Handmade pottery. Pottery with brushstrokes and imperfections. Food cooked and served by a person. In-person experiences. Not because AI can't replicate them, but because people will choose to value the human version. We've spent decades optimizing efficiency, scale, and output at the cost of connection, creativity, and experience. This might be the correction. And if nobody values that? Then yeah, we're doomed. But I don't think that's where it goes.

cards.title: AI ROI and the cost of not knowing
questions: what do you think most ai projects get wrong?
how do you measure ai roi
what is the roi of ai
how do you justify an ai project
cards.answer: People box ROI into time saved, cost reduced, revenue generated. That's incomplete. One of AI's most underrated capabilities is extracting insight that was previously inaccessible. What are the things you don't know? What are you losing because you didn't know them? That's the cost of not knowing, and it's where AI really earns its place. My legislation work is the clearest example. Being aware of what's being proposed before it passes lets you prevent losses and find opportunities. In HR, detecting where roles are shrinking or growing ahead of time is strategic intelligence. Not time. Not cost. Better decisions, better strategy, better plans.

cards.title: The model needs to know what the data means
questions: how do you evaluate an llm or a rag system? what metrics do you trust?
does an llm need a data dictionary
why does metadata matter for ai
how do you give a model schema context
cards.answer: Even if the data is technically correct, if the model doesn't understand what the fields represent, it'll produce confident garbage. Poorly named columns, encoded values with no explanation, missing metadata, no documentation, all of it breaks the system quietly. You need a context layer: a data dictionary or 'data cookbook,' metadata descriptions, schema explanations embedded into prompts. It needs to know what each field represents, how fields relate, and what the data is actually capturing. Without that you're asking it to interpret something it doesn't understand, and it'll happily make something up.

cards.title: The real risks of self-hosting models
questions: local open-weights models versus cloud apis: when do you choose which?
should we self host a model
downsides of running your own model
what are the drawbacks of self hosting
cards.answer: Some of these risks are still unknown. There's always potential for things getting hacked into. Maintenance overhead. Infrastructure complexity. Older or smaller models have logic and reasoning that's nowhere near the frontier. But it's a trade-off. Sometimes you don't need the frontier. It's about what you need and what the trade-offs are. Don't self-host because it sounds cooler. Self-host because the use case requires the control.

cards.title: Small models are good enough for most tasks
questions: local open-weights models versus cloud apis: when do you choose which?
do you need the biggest llm
do i need a frontier model
is the biggest model always better
cards.answer: A lot of tasks don't need advanced reasoning. Named entity extraction. Classification. Structured parsing. Pulling who was mentioned in a sentence. You don't need hyper-powerful reasoning for that. Smaller open models are faster, cheaper, and good enough. Match the tool to the task. Not everything needs the most powerful LLM available. Using Llama for what I'm using it for is exactly right.

cards.title: My real strengths
questions: what are you best at doing
cards.answer: Initiative, drive, ambition. I move fast and I'm action-oriented, 'this is the problem, here's how we fix it, let's go.' I'm good at getting people fired up, not by pushing but by asking what they think we should do and then backing their idea with conviction. I'm a good communicator. I try to connect with stakeholders as humans first, not by leading with numbers or solutions. And I'm a leader, but not a boss. I lead through enthusiasm, not hard deadlines.

cards.title: Where I add the most value on a team
questions: what's your communication style? how do you like to work with a team?
where do you add value on a team
what role do you play on a team
how do you lead a team
what kind of leader are you
cards.answer: Leadership. Planning, strategy, forward thinking, broad-level systems view. I'm good at getting teams to collaborate across departments, at delegating, at spotting where pieces connect. I lead with care. I think what matters is people feeling valued, learning, growing, with a sustainable workload. If someone needs to step back, fine. If we need more people, we hire. The goal isn't strict deadlines, it's real momentum.

cards.title: The most underrated thing in AI
questions: what's the most underrated idea in ai right now?
what is the most underrated thing in ai
what do companies overlook with ai
cards.answer: Fundamental data work. Governance, standardization, clean collection practices, metadata, schema design. Unsexy. Critical. For the next 3 to 5 years, the companies that win with AI will be the ones who did the foundational data work. Important datasets will get cleaned, collection will improve, and AI will eventually help with that cleaning. But right now it's manual, and it's the bottleneck.

cards.title: My general vibe
questions: three words friends would use to describe you?
what do you like in general
cards.answer: I prefer things that feel real, imperfect, and human over things that feel overly polished or artificial.

cards.title: What I actually want to build
questions: what would you build if you had a year and no constraints?
what do you want to build
what kind of projects do you want
what matters to you in your work
cards.answer: Things that make life better for people, or things I genuinely enjoy building. I want to look back at my career and feel something. One example I think about: the legislation work, making long, dense bills searchable and understandable so people could actually know what's being passed before it's passed. That's democracy-enhancing. That matters. I won't spend time on projects whose only value is squeezing more money out of customers, no matter how profitable.

cards.title: People will be paid to watch agents work
questions: what would a good transition to an ai world look like?
what new jobs will ai create
how long will the ai transition take
cards.answer: Within the next couple of years, a real category of job will be 'make sure the AI agent is still working.' Monitor health checks. Validate outputs. Catch silent failures. Keep the system running. Not glamorous, but real. The transition period (5 to 10 years) is going to be messy, role shifting, temporary inefficiencies, skill/demand mismatches. It's a transition phase, not the final state.

cards.title: What makes me different
questions: what kind of problems do you love working on? what makes a problem interesting to you?
why are you different from other data scientists
cards.answer: I genuinely believe nothing is impossible, it's just a question of how. I'd rather build something from scratch and open-source than rely on a big platform for a service we could build better ourselves. I'm also genuinely enthusiastic. A lot of people show up and do the work. I get actually excited about what we could build next.

cards.title: AI and what makes us human
questions: what does staying human look like while working with ai every day?
does ai make things feel empty
cards.answer: AI can produce technically perfect outputs, and that's exactly what makes them feel empty. Meaning comes from the fact that a human made something. The typo, the brushstroke, the voice cracking, that's what makes it real. AI doesn't replace that. It highlights it. If anything, automation should free us up for the things that are uniquely human: connection, creativity, expression. When everything becomes automated, authenticity is what matters, not perfection.

cards.title: What I understand that others miss
questions: how do you decide whether an ai system is good enough to ship? how do you know it works?
what do others miss about ai
how do you know an ai result is right
the job of a data scientist now
what do people miss about ai results
ai output that looks right but is wrong
cards.answer: In the AI era, things look convincingly right even when they're wrong. Code generation is fast. Analysis is fast. But so much of it is wrong in subtle ways. The real job now is validation, combing through line by line, column by column, asking where the data came from, whether it makes sense. If I'm getting 100% accuracy on a model, something is wrong. If everything is falling into place too easily, something is wrong. The job of a data scientist now is to slow it down.

cards.title: When something isn't worth fixing
questions: how do you approach a problem nobody has solved before? walk through your process.
when is data not worth cleaning
how do you know when to stop
when do you give up on a fix
cards.answer: If each new rule only fixes a tiny percentage of the data, the approach isn't scalable. The issue isn't cleaning anymore, it's structural. Always ask: will this generalize? If not, it's probably not worth the effort.

cards.title: My path into cognitive science
questions: why cognitive science, and how did you get from there to ai?
how did you get into cognitive science
how did you get into ai
cards.answer: I worked in service and hospitality in Austin, Texas, including a couple of years at Casino El Camino. I moved back to San Diego and spent my first year going all in on art but realized it wasn't going to pay the bills. I worked at Starbucks while putting myself through school at MiraCosta College, taking rigorous math to prepare for engineering. I transferred to UC San Diego for nanoengineering but switched to cognitive science for its breadth: data science, coding, neuroscience, psychology, child development, the brain, even art. I still love it. I have real interest in a PhD in cognitive science at UC San Diego but I am so productive teaching myself and building things that I am not sure school is in my best interest unless it meant hands-on work in a research lab.

cards.title: Favorite bands
